extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian philosophy, scholars of aesthetics and teleology, and educated general readers seeking an introduction to Kant's Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Kant's criteria for aesthetic and teleological judgements as presented in the Editor's Introduction and related exposition in the Critique of Judgement. Focuses on what makes judgments of beauty, the sublime, art, genius, and teleology valid or characteristic in Kant's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste is a judgement about feeling (pleasure or displeasure) rather than about cognition or concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differentiates aesthetic judgement from logical or moral judgement: it concerns the feeling of pleasure and its relation to the object, not a determinate concept or empirical interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of the satisfaction determining judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction which determines a judgement of taste is disinterested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure judgement of taste requires that the pleasure be free from personal desires, practical interest, or inclination to possess the object; contrasted with the pleasant and the good, both of which are bound up with interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in the pleasant is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure classified as 'pleasant' is tied to private or empirical interest rather than disinterested aesthetic appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This serves as an anti-pattern for pure aesthetic judgement: if liking an object is due to desire or appetite, it is not a pure judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in the good is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction in judgments about the good is connected to practical interest, i.e., it presupposes ends and concepts of worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgements of moral or practical goodness differ from aesthetic judgements because they are conceptually grounded and tied to interests and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful as object of universal satisfaction apart from concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is that which, apart from concepts, is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement of taste claims universal validity (we think others should agree) even though it is not based on a determinate concept; this 'universality' is subjective in Kant's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of satisfaction in judgement of taste is subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality we ascribe to a judgement of taste is represented only as subjective, not as an objective rule derived from concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant explains this by appeal to a presupposed sensus communis (common sense) — a shared faculty structure that grounds communicability of aesthetic feeling; this is a subjective necessity represented as if objective under that presupposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without definite purpose (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic of the object called beautiful is that it betrays a purposiveness without a definite purpose; the judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of purposiveness of an object (or its mode of representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes aesthetic purposiveness (form harmonising with faculties) from teleological purposiveness (adaptation to an end). The object appears 'as if' purposive, but no explicit purpose is asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgements rest on a priori grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on a priori grounds; there are a priori principles underlying aesthetic judgement as there are for understanding and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues for an a priori philosophy of pleasure: certain structural relations between faculties make aesthetic judgement possible prior to empirical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste independent of charm and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion (and of mere sensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and elucidation: charms of sense or emotional associations contaminate pure aesthetic judgement; a pure judgement isolates form and the free play of faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure aesthetic judgement independent of the concept of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is quite independent of the concept of perfection; pleasure in beauty is distinct from pleasure in perfection or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differentiates aesthetic appreciation from judgments based on correctness, usefulness, or perfection, which are conceptually driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free beauty vs dependent beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement of the beautiful is 'free' (not tied to a determinate concept), whereas a judgement that an object is beautiful under a definite concept is not pure (dependent beauty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free beauty engages aesthetic judgement alone; dependent beauty is appreciated relative to an idea or concept (e.g., beauty of a beautiful house because it fulfils a concept of house).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of aesthetic satisfaction is exemplary and presupposes sensus communis
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity ascribed to judgements of taste is not theoretical or practical but 'exemplary' — we set our satisfaction as an example to others, presupposing a common sense (sensus communis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicability of aesthetic feeling and the presupposition that cognitive faculties are comparable in others underpin the subjective claim to universal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective principle of taste possible
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no objective principle of taste possible; the principle of Taste is the subjective principle of Judgement in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's anti‑pattern: attempts to found taste on objective rules fail because aesthetic judgement makes subjective universal claims without concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement involves communicability of sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste presupposes that the sensation (feeling) involved is communicable to others; taste functions as a kind of sensus communis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This feature is central to Kant's Deduction of aesthetic judgements and to accounting for the claim to universal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sublime resides in the subject, not in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity really resides in the mind: the feeling of the Sublime expresses a purposiveness of the subject in respect of the object; nothing in nature is sublime in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with beauty: beauty is in form restful to the faculties; the sublime involves a mental movement excited by formlessness or magnitude that reveals the supersensible capacity of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between the mathematically and dynamically Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematically Sublime concerns magnitude (the absolutely great), while the dynamically Sublime concerns power (Nature regarded as might).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each kind yields different feelings and modes of satisfaction; the mathematically sublime evokes ideas of magnitude beyond sensible comprehension, the dynamically sublime evokes moral/security responses to overpowering might.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of the Sublime awakens a sense of the supersensible (moral) destination of man
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of the Sublime awakens in us a feeling of the supersensible destination of man; it indicates a mental faculty that surpasses sense and is tied to moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant connects the universality of judgements on the sublime to the presupposition of moral feeling in humans; appreciation of the sublime has ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime involves pain without actual fear; must exclude extraneous charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects called sublime inspire a feeling of pain rather than pleasure but must not inspire actual fear; no extraneous charm must mingle with the satisfaction if the judgement is to remain pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: if fear is real or charm intervenes, the judgement is not a pure judgement of the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine art as the art of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art is regarded as the art of Genius: an innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art (§46).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius is the faculty of presenting aesthetical Ideas to which no concept is adequate; the great artist cannot fully communicate methods or rules, and so art differs from science by absence of definite concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius cannot be taught and must be regulated by taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius (poeta nascitur, non fit) cannot be taught or fully explained by rules; yet genius requires to be kept in check by taste — better to lose something of genius than to violate the canons of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a normative relation: innovation and originality are valuable but must not transgress the regulative standards of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art is art in so far as it seems like nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art is an art in so far as it seems like nature; beautiful art is the art of genius and often seems to follow natural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's value tied to how it evokes purposiveness like nature; this grounds aesthetic appreciation of artistic imitation or harmony with perceived natural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Ideas exceed conceptual expression
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetical Idea is an intuition of the imagination to which no concept is adequate; more is present in the productions of genius than can be perfectly expressed in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why great art resists full conceptual explanation — it evokes intuitive ideas beyond conceptualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement: objective purposiveness of nature (formal vs material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological judgements concern the objective purposiveness of nature; Kant distinguishes purposiveness that is merely formal from that which is material (i.e., purposiveness as adaptation to definite ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal purposiveness relates to the form fitting our cognitive faculties; material purposiveness relates to actual adaptation to ends (organised beings). The distinction guides whether we infer design or merely ascribe purposiveness for reflective purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings as natural purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Things regarded as natural purposes are organised beings: in such products of nature every part exists by means of the other parts and is thought as existing for the sake of the others and the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion underlies the special status of biological organisation in teleological explanation and motivates Kant’s claim that teleology is a necessary regulative principle for studying life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of judging internal purposiveness in organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of judging of internal purposiveness is that parts of organised beings are reciprocally means and ends (each part exists for the others and the whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the methodological guide for teleological investigation: we may need to judge nature ‘as if’ directed to ends when studying organisms, while remaining critical about asserting real external design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as a regulative principle of reflective judgement (not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of an objective purposiveness of nature is a critical principle of Reason for the reflective Judgement; teleology guides investigation but does not have constitutive objective validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant holds that teleology is necessary for scientific and practical inquiry into organisms and nature, yet its ultimate grounding (e.g., Theism) is only regulatively admissible, not provable as constitutive knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism vs Technic (mechanical explanation vs teleological explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a necessary distinction between mechanism (explanation by mechanical laws) and the Technic (purposive operation) of nature; Kant argues for the necessary subordination or interplay of mechanical to teleological principles when explaining natural purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant acknowledges mechanical explanations often suffice (e.g., crystallisation) but maintains that for organised beings teleological judgement is indispensable for intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology leads to Theism as the only fully satisfactory explanation (but only regulatively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the logically possible doctrines to account for purposiveness, Theism represents natural purposes as produced by the Will and Design of an intelligent Author and Governor; it is 'superior' as an explanation but valid only as a regulative principle, not as constitutive knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant presents Theism as the most satisfactory human explanation for purposiveness while insisting we cannot claim it as objective metaphysical proof — it serves speculative and practical use of Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: The analytic/deduction method for aesthetic judgement (investigate communicability and faculty relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's method for the deduction of aesthetic judgements involves investigating the communicability of sensation and the relations of cognitive faculties that make taste possible (the sensus communis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is procedural guidance: to justify the subjective universality of taste, show how the structure of faculties explains communicable pleasure and the feeling of purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as symbol of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant posits a connection between beauty and goodness: Beauty can serve as a symbol of morality; the capacity to appreciate beauty is a mark of a moral disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He does not claim this allows direct inference about the character of the art connoisseur, but links aesthetic sensibility with moral feeling, especially in the appreciation of the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating aesthetic judgement with empirical associations (colour as extraneous charm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant asserts that colour in a picture may be only an extraneous charm and can distract from the beauty of form; pure aesthetic judgement should isolate formal purposiveness from sensory charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: weighting merely sensory charms (colour, ornament) as constitutive of beauty contradicts the aim of a pure judgement of taste focused on form and purposiveness.
